analysis.one_liner: Stabilizes Obamacare markets with reinsurance, adds a government-run public insurance option, expands subsidies, and lets Medicare negotiate drug prices.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced past its referral to the Senate Finance Committee and died when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019, with no cosponsors and no committee vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have put federal money into covering the most expensive patients so premiums for everyone else drop, created a government-run insurance plan sold alongside private plans on the Obamacare exchanges, extended premium subsidies to higher incomes, expanded help with out-of-pocket costs, and taken on drug prices by requiring manufacturer rebates for low-income Medicare enrollees and letting the government negotiate Medicare drug prices. It was introduced by one senator with no cosponsors, referred to the Finance Committee, and never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: People who buy their own health insurance on the marketplaces would benefit from lower premiums (reinsurance), bigger tax credits (eligibility extended to 600% of poverty), and smaller deductibles (enhanced cost-sharing reductions). Seniors would benefit from Medicare negotiating drug prices, required manufacturer rebates for low-income enrollees, and a $37/month government-run drug plan. Medicaid patients would gain from a 100% federal match for integrated behavioral health care.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Marketplace enrollees, seniors on Medicare, Medicaid patients

how_it_helps.text: Establishes a permanent Individual Market Reinsurance Fund that reimburses insurers 80% of claims between $50,000 and $450,000 for high-cost patients, lowering premiums for everyone else buying coverage on their own.
Creates a government-run public health insurance option sold on the marketplaces, priced to compete with private insurers, to give consumers a benchmark alternative.
Raises the income ceiling for premium tax credits from 400% to 600% of the poverty line, so middle-income families priced out of marketplace coverage could get help.
Deepens cost-sharing reductions so lower- and middle-income enrollees' plans cover 85–95% of their medical costs, cutting deductibles and copays.

Restores Medicaid-style rebates for drugs dispensed to low-income Medicare enrollees and strikes the 'noninterference' clause so the government can negotiate Part D drug prices directly with manufacturers.
Offers seniors a nationwide government-run prescription drug plan with a $37 monthly premium as a low-price benchmark against private Part D plans.
Gives states a 100% federal match for Medicaid services delivered through team-based collaborative care models that integrate behavioral health into primary care.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers would fund the reinsurance fund, outreach grants, and cost-sharing subsidies. Brand-name drug manufacturers would pay new rebates and accept price negotiation, and private insurers would face a government-run competitor.

drawbacks.text: The bill cost the federal government real money: it appropriates 'such sums as are necessary' for reinsurance payments to insurers covering expensive patients, plus $500 million a year for outreach grants and $2 billion in start-up funding for the public option, with no dedicated revenue source named in the bill.

The public option would pay doctors and hospitals Medicare rates, which are lower than private insurance rates; providers argued this could shift costs or narrow choices, and the plan's ability to attract enrollment depended on that price advantage.

The public option bars administrative or judicial review of its payment rates, meaning providers could not challenge how the Secretary set rates — a design choice that concentrated decision-making in one agency.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits were broad and concrete: lower premiums for marketplace customers, expanded subsidies, cheaper drugs for seniors, and better mental health access. The costs were real but ordinary: federal spending on reinsurance, expanded tax credits, and cost-sharing reductions, plus drug manufacturer profits trimmed by rebates and negotiation. There is a fair design objection — the reinsurance fund shields insurers from losses on expensive patients, which puts taxpayer money at work protecting private companies — but the bill pairs that shield with a public competitor and drug price negotiation to hold insurers and drugmakers accountable, a more balanced package than reinsurance alone. On balance, the upside for families and seniors substantially outweighed the fiscal cost.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee on June 29, 2017, and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: The Senate introduced S. 1511 on June 29, 2017, and referred it the same day to the Committee on Finance.
No senator signed on as a cosponsor.
The bill's action history ends with that referral; no further action of any kind was taken during the 115th Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and drug manufacturers kept the status quo: no public option, no Medicare drug price negotiation, no rebate expansion. Middle-income families paying high premiums and seniors paying high drug prices got nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers and drugmakers; status quo held

for.name: Sen. Benjamin Cardin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and had it referred to the Senate Finance Committee.

against.name: Senate Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the floor or supported its consideration; the bill died in committee during a Republican-controlled Senate.

sides.party_line_note: No votes or floor action ever occurred; the only observable partisan fact is that a Democratic senator introduced it with zero cosponsors of either party in a Republican-controlled Senate.

industries.note: The reinsurance fund pays insurers for expensive enrollees, locking in private insurers as the channel for marketplace coverage, and the bill directs hundreds of millions in outreach grants into the enrollment system. At the same time the public option would compete with them, cutting both ways.

The bill restores Medicaid-style rebates for low-income Medicare enrollees, empowers the government to negotiate Part D prices, and would bar drugs from coverage if the manufacturer refuses a rebate agreement — a direct hit to drug company revenue.
The public option would pay Medicare rates, which are lower than private rates, reducing provider revenue; the Medicaid behavioral health match would increase funding for care delivery.

industries.industry: Pharmacy benefit and behavioral health providers
industries.note: The 100% federal match for collaborative care and integration of behavioral health into primary care would expand demand for these services.
